claim: Keratin 14 (K14) provides vital structural support in basal keratinocytes of epidermis.
source: The intermediate filament protein keratin 14 (K14) provides vital structural support in basal keratinocytes of epidermis.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about keratin function.

claim: K14-dependent disulfide bonding plays a role in the organization and dynamics of keratin IFs in skin keratinocytes.
source: Recent studies evidenced a role for K14-dependent disulfide bonding in the organization and dynamics of keratin IFs in skin keratinocytes.
evidence: This claim references recent studies, indicating citation-based support.

claim: Knock-in mice harboring a cysteine-to-alanine substitution at Krt14's codon 373 (C373A) exhibit alterations in disulfide-bonded K14 species.
source: Here we report that knock-in mice harboring a cysteine-to-alanine substitution at Krt14's codon 373 (C373A) exhibit alterations in disulfide-bonded K14 species and a barrier defect secondary to enhanced proliferation, faster transit time and altered differentiation in epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Krt14 C373A mice exhibit a barrier defect secondary to enhanced proliferation, faster transit time and altered differentiation in epidermis.
source: Here we report that knock-in mice harboring a cysteine-to-alanine substitution at Krt14's codon 373 (C373A) exhibit alterations in disulfide-bonded K14 species and a barrier defect secondary to enhanced proliferation, faster transit time and altered differentiation in epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: A proteomics screen identified 14-3-3 as K14 interacting proteins.
source: A proteomics screen identified 14-3-3 as K14 interacting proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: YAP1, a transcriptional effector of Hippo signaling regulated by 14-3-3sigma in skin keratinocytes, shows aberrant subcellular partitioning and function in differentiating Krt14 C373A keratinocytes.
source: Follow-up studies showed that YAP1, a transcriptional effector of Hippo signaling regulated by 14-3-3sigma in skin keratinocytes, shows aberrant subcellular partitioning and function in differentiating Krt14 C373A keratinocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D and gene expression data in Figure 4E.

claim: Residue C373 in K14 is conserved in a subset of keratins.
source: Residue C373 in K14, which is conserved in a subset of keratins, is revealed as a novel regulator of keratin organization and YAP function in early differentiating keratinocytes, with an impact on cell mechanics, homeostasis and barrier function in epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Residue C373 in K14 is a novel regulator of keratin organization and YAP function in early differentiating keratinocytes.
source: Residue C373 in K14, which is conserved in a subset of keratins, is revealed as a novel regulator of keratin organization and YAP function in early differentiating keratinocytes, with an impact on cell mechanics, homeostasis and barrier function in epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript, including Figures 3-6.

claim: Residue C373 in K14 has an impact on cell mechanics, homeostasis and barrier function in epidermis.
source: Residue C373 in K14, which is conserved in a subset of keratins, is revealed as a novel regulator of keratin organization and YAP function in early differentiating keratinocytes, with an impact on cell mechanics, homeostasis and barrier function in epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on TEWL measurements (Figure 2C), proliferation and differentiation markers (Figure 3), and mechanosensing readouts (Figure 6).

claim: The epidermis maintains a vital and multidimensional barrier to water and the outside environment while renewing itself with rapid kinetics.
source: The epidermis covering our skin and body maintains a vital and multidimensional barrier to water and the outside environment while renewing itself with rapid kinetics, even under normal physiological conditions (Kubo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kubo et al., 2012.

claim: Keratin intermediate filaments are major protein constituents in epithelial cells and are encoded by a large family of 54 conserved genes.
source: Keratin intermediate filaments are major protein constituents in epithelial cells and are encoded by a large family of 54 conserved genes that are individually regulated in a tissue- and differentiation-specific fashion (Schweizer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schweizer et al., 2006.

claim: Keratin genes are individually regulated in a tissue- and differentiation-specific fashion.
source: Keratin intermediate filaments are major protein constituents in epithelial cells and are encoded by a large family of 54 conserved genes that are individually regulated in a tissue- and differentiation-specific fashion (Schweizer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schweizer et al., 2006.

claim: Type I keratin 14 (K14) and type II K5 co-polymerize to form the prominent IF apparatus in the progenitor basal layer of epidermis and related complex epithelia.
source: The type I keratin 14 (K14) and type II K5 co-polymerize to form the prominent IF apparatus that occurs in the progenitor basal layer of epidermis and related complex epithelia (Nelson and Sun, 1983; Fuchs, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nelson and Sun, 1983 and Fuchs, 1995.

claim: K5-K14 IFs provide structural support and mechanical resilience to keratinocytes in the basal layer of epidermis and related epithelia.
source: First, to provide structural support and mechanical resilience to keratinocytes in the basal layer of epidermis and related epithelia (Coulombe et al., 1991a; Vassar et al., 1991; Fuchs and Coulombe, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coulombe et al., 1991a; Vassar et al., 1991; Fuchs and Coulombe, 1992.

claim: K5-K14 IFs regulate the distribution of melanin with an impact on skin pigmentation and tone.
source: Second, to regulate the distribution of melanin with an impact on skin pigmentation and tone (Uttam et al., 1996; Betz et al., 2006; Gu and Coulombe, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Uttam et al., 1996; Betz et al., 2006; Gu and Coulombe, 2007.

claim: Dominantly-acting missense alleles in either KRT5 or KRT14 underlie the vast majority of cases of epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS).
source: Dominantly-acting missense alleles in either KRT5 or KRT14 underlie the vast majority of cases of epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS), a rare genetic skin disorder in which trivial trauma results in skin blistering secondary to the lysis of fragile basal keratinocytes (Bonifas et al., 1991; Coulombe et al., 1991b; Fuchs and Coulombe, 1992; Lane et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonifas et al., 1991; Coulombe et al., 1991b; Fuchs and Coulombe, 1992; Lane et al., 1992.

claim: The crystal structure of the interacting 2B regions of corresponding rod domain segments in human K5 and K14 highlighted the presence of a trans-dimer, homotypic disulfide bond involving cysteine (C) residue 367 (C367) in K14.
source: Structural insight gained from solving the crystal structure of the interacting 2B regions of corresponding rod domain segments in human K5 and K14 highlighted the presence of a trans-dimer, homotypic disulfide bond involving cysteine (C) residue 367 (C367) in K14 (Coulombe and Lee, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coulombe and Lee, 2012.

claim: Residue C367 in K14 occurs within a four-residue interruption, or stutter, in the long-range heptad repeat of coil two in the central alpha-helical rod domain in virtually all IF proteins.
source: Conspicuously, residue C367 in K14 occurs within a four-residue interruption, or stutter, in the long-range heptad repeat of coil two in the central alpha-helical rod domain in virtually all IF proteins (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: K14 C367-dependent disulfides form in human and mouse skin keratinocytes.
source: We showed that K14 C367-dependent disulfides form in human and mouse skin keratinocytes (Lee et al., 2012), where they play a role in the assembly, organization and steady state dynamics of keratin IFs in live skin keratinocytes (Feng and Coulombe, 2015a; Feng and Coulombe, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012; Feng and Coulombe, 2015a; Feng and Coulombe, 2015b.

claim: K14 C367-dependent disulfides play a role in the assembly, organization and steady state dynamics of keratin IFs in live skin keratinocytes.
source: We showed that K14 C367-dependent disulfides form in human and mouse skin keratinocytes (Lee et al., 2012), where they play a role in the assembly, organization and steady state dynamics of keratin IFs in live skin keratinocytes (Feng and Coulombe, 2015a; Feng and Coulombe, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feng and Coulombe, 2015a; Feng and Coulombe, 2015b.

claim: Loss of the stutter cysteine alters K14's ability to become part of the dense meshwork of keratin filaments that occurs in the perinuclear space of early differentiating keratinocytes.
source: We also showed that loss of the stutter cysteine alters K14's ability to become part of the dense meshwork of keratin filaments that occurs in the perinuclear space of early differentiating keratinocytes (Lee et al., 2012; Feng and Coulombe, 2015a; Feng and Coulombe, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012; Feng and Coulombe, 2015a; Feng and Coulombe, 2015b.

claim: The stutter cysteine in K14 protein regulates entry into differentiation and the balance between proliferation and differentiation through regulated interactions with 14-3-3 adaptor proteins and YAP1.
source: Here, we report on studies involving a new mouse model that provides evidence that the stutter cysteine in K14 protein regulates entry into differentiation and thus the balance between proliferation and differentiation through regulated interactions with 14-3-3 adaptor proteins and YAP1, a terminal effector of Hippo signaling (Pocaterra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 4-6.

claim: YAP1 is a terminal effector of Hippo signaling.
source: Here, we report on studies involving a new mouse model that provides evidence that the stutter cysteine in K14 protein regulates entry into differentiation and thus the balance between proliferation and differentiation through regulated interactions with 14-3-3 adaptor proteins and YAP1, a terminal effector of Hippo signaling (Pocaterra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pocaterra et al., 2020.

claim: Codon C367 in KRT14 (human) occurs at position 373 in Krt14 (mouse).
source: Codon C367 in KRT14 (human) occurs at position 373 in Krt14 (mouse), and is conserved in the orthologous keratin of several other species (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Codon C367 in KRT14 (human) is conserved in the orthologous keratin of several other species.
source: Codon C367 in KRT14 (human) occurs at position 373 in Krt14 (mouse), and is conserved in the orthologous keratin of several other species (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Codon C367 in KRT14 (human) is conserved in many other type I keratin genes expressed in skin.
source: Moreover, this codon is also conserved in many other type I keratin genes expressed in skin (Strnad et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Strnad et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012 and sequence alignment data in Figure 1B.

claim: Krt14 C373A mice are born in the expected mendelian ratio.
source: Krt14 C373A mice are born in the expected mendelian ratio, are viable and fertile, and show a normal body weight when reaching adulthood (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Krt14 C373A mice are viable and fertile.
source: Krt14 C373A mice are born in the expected mendelian ratio, are viable and fertile, and show a normal body weight when reaching adulthood (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Krt14 C373A mice show a normal body weight when reaching adulthood.
source: Krt14 C373A mice are born in the expected mendelian ratio, are viable and fertile, and show a normal body weight when reaching adulthood (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Steady state levels of K14 protein are unaffected in Krt14 C373A relative to WT skin.
source: Analysis of total skin proteins from several body sites showed that steady state levels of K14 protein are unaffected in Krt14 C373A relative to WT skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The pattern of K14-dependent, high molecular weight disulfide-bonded species is markedly altered in Krt14 C373A relative to WT skin, with fewer species that occur at lower levels.
source: By contrast, the pattern of K14-dependent, high molecular weight disulfide-bonded species is markedly altered, given fewer species that occur at lower levels (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The alteration in K14-dependent disulfide bonding is especially pronounced in ear and tail skin of Krt14 C373A mice.
source: This is so especially in ear and tail skin (Figure 1F,G), prompting us to focus on these two body sites in subsequent analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The residual K14-dependent disulfide bonding occurring in Krt14 C373A mutant skin likely reflects the participation of cysteines located in the N-terminal domain of K14.
source: The residual K14-dependent disulfide bonding occurring in Krt14 C373A mutant skin (Figure 1F,G) likely reflects the participation of cysteines located in the N-terminal domain of K14 (see Figure 1A and Feng and Coulombe, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data in Figure 1F,G and citation to Feng and Coulombe, 2015a.

claim: The epidermis of Krt14 C373A mice is modestly but significantly thickened relative to WT in ear and tail skin.
source: By histology, the epidermis of Krt14 C373A mice is modestly but significantly thickened relative to WT in ear and tail skin (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) is increased in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT control at baseline.
source: Measurement of trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) at the skin surface revealed an increase in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT control. This is so both at baseline (7.02 ± 0.72 g/m2/h vs. 2.95 ± 0.49 g/m2/h) and after topical acetone application (19.20 ± 1.78 g/m2/h vs. 7.02 ± 0.72 g/m2/h) (Figure 2C), a standard challenge that puts the skin barrier under a mild and reversible stress (Denda et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEWL measurement data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) is increased in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT control after topical acetone application.
source: Measurement of trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) at the skin surface revealed an increase in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT control. This is so both at baseline (7.02 ± 0.72 g/m2/h vs. 2.95 ± 0.49 g/m2/h) and after topical acetone application (19.20 ± 1.78 g/m2/h vs. 7.02 ± 0.72 g/m2/h) (Figure 2C), a standard challenge that puts the skin barrier under a mild and reversible stress (Denda et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEWL measurement data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Topical acetone application is a standard challenge that puts the skin barrier under a mild and reversible stress.
source: Measurement of trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) at the skin surface revealed an increase in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT control. This is so both at baseline (7.02 ± 0.72 g/m2/h vs. 2.95 ± 0.49 g/m2/h) and after topical acetone application (19.20 ± 1.78 g/m2/h vs. 7.02 ± 0.72 g/m2/h) (Figure 2C), a standard challenge that puts the skin barrier under a mild and reversible stress (Denda et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Denda et al., 1996.

claim: Skin barrier defects often trigger elevated expression of Danger-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs).
source: Skin barrier defects often trigger elevated expression of Danger-Associated Molecular Patterns (Lessard et al., 2013) (DAMPs, also known as alarmins).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lessard et al., 2013.

claim: At baseline, DAMPs such as S100a8, S100a9, Mmp9, and Ptgs2 are upregulated by 4-fold or more at the mRNA level in Krt14 C373A skin compared to WT.
source: At baseline, DAMPs such as S100a8, S100a9, Mmp9, and Ptgs2 are upregulated by 4-fold or more at the mRNA level in Krt14 C373A skin compared to WT (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The aberrant upregulation of DAMPs in Krt14 C373A skin is markedly enhanced after a topical acetone challenge to the barrier.
source: This aberrant state is markedly enhanced after a topical acetone challenge to the barrier (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cornified envelopes (CEs) are key contributors to skin barrier function.
source: Next, we analyzed cornified envelopes (CEs) isolated from epidermis, given that they are key contributors to skin barrier function (Eckhart et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eckhart et al., 2013.

claim: CEs harvested from WT mice appear relatively uniform in size and shape, are mostly oval-shaped, and feature clear and smooth outlines.
source: CEs harvested from WT mice appear relatively uniform in size and shape, are mostly oval-shaped, and feature clear and smooth outlines (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: CEs isolated from Krt14 C373A mice are smaller (85% of the area and 87% of the circumference of WT CEs), jagged, and less oval-shaped (aspect ratio of 1.3 compared to 1.1 in WT).
source: By contrast, CEs isolated from Krt14 C373A mice are smaller (85% of the area and 87% of the circumference of WT CEs), jagged, and less oval-shaped (aspect ratio of 1.3 compared to 1.1 in WT) (Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and quantitative data shown in Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: At 2 hr after a single pulse of EdU, a significantly greater fraction of keratinocytes are labeled in the basal layer of Krt14 C373A epidermis compared to WT (by ~1.6 fold; p=0.024).
source: At 2 hr after a single pulse of the nucleotide analog Edu (Chehrehasa et al., 2009), a significantly greater fraction of keratinocytes are labeled in the basal layer of Krt14 C373A epidermis compared to WT (by ~1.6 fold; p=0.024) (Figure 3A,B), indicating that keratinocyte proliferation is enhanced at baseline in mutant mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Keratinocyte proliferation is enhanced at baseline in Krt14 C373A mutant mice.
source: At 2 hr after a single pulse of the nucleotide analog Edu (Chehrehasa et al., 2009), a significantly greater fraction of keratinocytes are labeled in the basal layer of Krt14 C373A epidermis compared to WT (by ~1.6 fold; p=0.024) (Figure 3A,B), indicating that keratinocyte proliferation is enhanced at baseline in mutant mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Following a 1 day chase after the Edu pulse, the difference in EdU labeling between WT and Krt14 C373A is accentuated (>2 fold; p=0.01).
source: Following a 1 day chase after the Edu pulse, this difference is accentuated (>2 fold; p=0.01) and Edu-labeled nuclei now occur in the suprabasal layers of epidermis in both genotypes, reflecting keratinocyte exit from the basal layer (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Following a 3-day chase after the Edu pulse, there are significantly more Edu-labeled nuclei in the suprabasal layers of Krt14 C373A epidermis compared to WT.
source: Following a 3-day chase after the Edu pulse, nuclear labeling remains high and stable in the basal layer of epidermis in both genotypes, but a clear additional difference emerges as there are significantly more Edu-labeled nuclei in the suprabasal layers of mutant epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: At the 7-day mark after EdU pulse, the suprabasal epidermis of Krt14 C373A skin shows far more labeled nuclei compared to WT.
source: At the 7-day mark, the fraction of labeled cells in the basal layer has subsided in both genotypes but, again, the suprabasal epidermis of Krt14 C373A skin shows far more labeled nuclei (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Keratinocytes in Krt14 C373A epidermis show enhanced proliferation confined to the basal layer at baseline.
source: This pulse-chase experiment shows that keratinocytes in Krt14 C373A epidermis show enhanced proliferation confined to the basal layer at baseline, and that keratinocytes exhibit a faster pace of movement across the suprabasal layers as they progress through differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the EdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Keratinocytes in Krt14 C373A epidermis exhibit a faster pace of movement across the suprabasal layers as they progress through differentiation.
source: This pulse-chase experiment shows that keratinocytes in Krt14 C373A epidermis show enhanced proliferation confined to the basal layer at baseline, and that keratinocytes exhibit a faster pace of movement across the suprabasal layers as they progress through differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the EdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: A similar phenotype of enhanced proliferation and faster transit has been previously described for Krt10 null mice.
source: A similar phenotype has been previously described for Krt10 null mice (Reichelt and Magin, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reichelt and Magin, 2002.

claim: There is a greater frequency (~3 fold) of TUNEL-positive nuclei in Krt14 C373A epidermis compared to WT, with apoptotic cell death confined to the suprabasal compartment.
source: We also observed a greater frequency (~3 fold) of TUNEL-positive nuclei in Krt14 C373A epidermis compared to WT, with apoptotic cell death confined to the suprabasal compartment (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: p63 is a master regulator of epidermal stratification and differentiation.
source: We also examined expression of p63, given its role as master regulator of epidermal stratification and differentiation (Soares and Zhou, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Soares and Zhou, 2018.

claim: A distinct immunostaining pattern for p63 was observed in Krt14 C373A epidermis relative to WT.
source: A distinct immunostaining pattern was observed in Krt14 C373A epidermis relative to WT (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: p63-positive staining shows a conspicuous elongated shape and extends higher up in the Krt14 C373A mutant epidermis compared to WT.
source: Upon quantitation, significant differences prevailed in terms of frequency of keratinocytes labeled and their distance from the basal lamina (Figure 3F), with p63-positive staining showing a conspicuous elongated shape and extending higher up in the mutant epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The staining for filaggrin and loricrin were markedly decreased (~62% and 48% reductions, respectively) in Krt14 C373A epidermis relative to WT.
source: The staining for filaggrin and loricrin were markedly decreased (~62% and 48% reductions, respectively) while the staining for K10 was modestly decreased (~37% reduction) in Krt14 C373A epidermis relative to WT (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: The staining for K10 was modestly decreased (~37% reduction) in Krt14 C373A epidermis relative to WT.
source: The staining for filaggrin and loricrin were markedly decreased (~62% and 48% reductions, respectively) while the staining for K10 was modestly decreased (~37% reduction) in Krt14 C373A epidermis relative to WT (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Claudin 3 staining was decreased by ~33% in Krt14 C373A epidermis, consistent with the barrier defect.
source: Claudin 3 staining was decreased by ~33% in Krt14 C373A epidermis, consistent with the barrier defect.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: The signals for E-cadherin and desmoplakin appeared slightly increased in Krt14 C373A epidermis.
source: The signals for E-cadherin and desmoplakin appeared slightly increased (Figure 3I), an occurrence that may reflect the modest epidermal thicknening (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Several markers including K14, K10, loricrin and filaggrin appear normal in the thin epidermis of back skin in Krt14 C373A mice.
source: In contrast to tail and ear epidermis, several markers including K14, K10, loricrin and filaggrin appear normal in the thin epidermis of back skin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with the markedly lower yield of K14-dependent disulfide bonding in this body site (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Replacing Cys with Ala at position 367 in human K14 does not abrogate 10 nm filament formation but leads to a reduction in the perinuclear clustering of keratin filaments in cultured keratinocytes.
source: We previously showed that replacing Cys with Ala at position 367 in human K14 does not abrogate 10 nm filament formation but leads to a reduction in the perinuclear clustering of keratin filaments in cultured keratinocytes (Feng and Coulombe, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feng and Coulombe, 2015b.

claim: In basal keratinocytes of WT epidermis, keratin IFs typically occur as bundles near the nucleus.
source: In basal keratinocytes of WT epidermis, keratin IFs typically occur as bundles near the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: In Krt14 C373A basal keratinocytes, keratin IFs are absent from the perinuclear region and appear redistributed towards the cell periphery.
source: In Krt14 C373A basal keratinocytes, however, keratin IFs are absent from the perinuclear region and appear redistributed towards the cell periphery (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: There is no ultrastructural evidence of cell fragility in Krt14 C373A epidermis.
source: Consistent with the macroscopic appearance of skin tissue there is no ultrastructural evidence of cell fragility in Krt14 C373A epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Nuclei in Krt14 C373A keratinocytes feature a more ellipsoid shape along with a greater frequency of cytoplasmic invaginations (by ~1.4 fold in basal keratinocytes and by ~1.7 fold in suprabasal keratinocytes) compared to WT controls.
source: We find that nuclei feature a more ellipsoid shape along with a greater frequency of cytoplasmic invaginations (by ~1.4 fold in basal keratinocytes and by ~1.7 fold in suprabasal keratinocytes, respectively) compared to WT controls; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy and quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 14-3-3σ and other 14-3-3 isoforms are major interacting partners for K14 in WT cell cultures.
source: This screen identified 14-3-3σ and other 14-4-3 isoforms as major interacting partners for K14 in WT cell cultures (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There is a strong precedent for interactions between 14-3-3 proteins and keratins, including K18 and K17, which occur in a phosphorylation-dependent fashion.
source: There is a strong precedent for interactions between 14-3-3 proteins and keratins, including K18 (Liao and Omary, 1996; Ku et al., 1998), K17 (Kim et al., 2006), which occur in a phosphorylation-dependent fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liao and Omary, 1996; Ku et al., 1998; Kim et al., 2006.

claim: Transfected, HA tagged-14-3-3σ physically interact with endogenous WT K14 and Krt14373A mutant protein in mouse keratinocytes in primary culture.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that transfected, HA tagged-14-3-3σ physically interact with endogenous WT K14 and Krt14373A mutant protein in mouse keratinocytes in primary culture (Figure 4B and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 14-3-3σ regulates the proliferation and differentiation of keratinocytes in epidermis.
source: 14-3-3σ was deemed of interest because it regulates the proliferation and differentiation of keratinocytes in epidermis (Herron et al., 2005; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herron et al., 2005; Li et al., 2005.

claim: 14-3-3σ modulates the cellular localization of YAP.
source: The latter is achieved in part by modulating the cellular localization of YAP (Li et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2015), a terminal effector of Hippo signaling (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Silvis et al., 2011; Sambandam et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2015.

claim: YAP is a terminal effector of Hippo signaling.
source: The latter is achieved in part by modulating the cellular localization of YAP (Li et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2015), a terminal effector of Hippo signaling (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Silvis et al., 2011; Sambandam et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Silvis et al., 2011; Sambandam et al., 2015.

claim: Hippo is an evolutionary conserved pathway with a primary role in regulating growth and homeostasis in organs and tissues.
source: Hippo is an evolutionary conserved pathway with a primary role in regulating growth and homeostasis in organs and tissues (Pocaterra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pocaterra et al., 2020.

claim: 14-3-3σ occurs mostly as aggregates in suprabasal keratinocytes of Krt14 C373A epidermis, in striking contrast to the diffuse distribution observed in WT controls.
source: 14-3-3σ occurs mostly as aggregates in suprabasal keratinocytes of Krt14 C373A epidermis, which is in striking contrast to the diffuse distribution observed in WT controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A strong signal for YAP occurs in both the nucleus and cytoplasm in basal keratinocytes, and otherwise YAP occurs as a weaker and diffuse signal in the cytoplasm (but is not seen in the nucleus) of suprabasal keratinocytes in WT epidermis.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Sambandam et al., 2015), a strong signal for YAP occurs in both the nucleus and cytoplasm in basal keratinocytes, and otherwise YAP occurs as a weaker and diffuse signal in the cytoplasm (but is not seen in the nucleus) of suprabasal keratinocytes in WT epidermis (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and citations to Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Sambandam et al., 2015.

claim: In Krt14 C373A epidermis, YAP localizes preferentially to nuclei in both basal and suprabasal keratinocytes.
source: In Krt14 C373A epidermis, strikingly, YAP localizes preferentially to nuclei in both basal and suprabasal keratinocytes, in a consistent fashion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The steady state levels for several known YAP target gene mRNAs, including Cyr61, Zeb1, Ctgf and Snail2, are markedly elevated in Krt14 C373A relative to WT skin.
source: Follow-up RT-qPCR assays show that the steady state levels for several known YAP target gene mRNAs, including Cyr61, Zeb1, Ctgf and Snail2, are markedly elevated in Krt14 C373A relative to WT skin (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The levels of endogenous YAP1 and Ser127-phosphorylated YAP1 are similar in WT and Krt14 C373A skin.
source: By western immunoblotting, the levels of endogenous YAP1 and Ser127-phosphorylated YAP1 are similar in WT and Krt14 C373A skin (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: K14-dependent disulfide bonding is low in the absence of calcium and rises over the course of days after adding calcium to primary cultures of WT mouse keratinocytes.
source: K14-dependent disulfide bonding is low in the absence of calcium and rises of the course of days after adding calcium to primary cultures of WT mouse keratinocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In the absence of calcium, the staining for YAP is concentrated in the nucleus in both WT and Krt14 C373A keratinocytes.
source: In the absence of calcium, the staining for YAP is concentrated in the nucleus in both WT and Krt14 C373A keratinocytes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: After addition of calcium (1 mM), 73% of WT keratinocytes lose their nuclear YAP signal whereas 95% of Krt14 C373A keratinocytes exhibit predominantly nuclear YAP.
source: After addition of calcium (1 mM), which triggers differentiation and mimics a suprabasal state (Hennings et al., 1980), 73% of WT keratinocytes lose their nuclear YAP signal whereas 95% of Krt14 C373A keratinocytes exhibit predominantly nuclear YAP (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Addition of calcium (1 mM) triggers differentiation and mimics a suprabasal state in keratinocytes.
source: After addition of calcium (1 mM), which triggers differentiation and mimics a suprabasal state (Hennings et al., 1980), 73% of WT keratinocytes lose their nuclear YAP signal whereas 95% of Krt14 C373A keratinocytes exhibit predominantly nuclear YAP (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hennings et al., 1980.

claim: Both K10 and filaggrin proteins occur at lower levels in calcium-treated primary cultures of Krt14 C373A relative to WT keratinocytes.
source: Western immunoblotting confirmed that, as expected, both K10 and filaggrin proteins occur at lower levels in calcium-treated primary cultures of Krt14 C373A relative to WT keratinocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting a delay or a defect in terminal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: PLA assays yielded evidence for decreased interactions between 14-3-3σ and YAP in Krt14 C373A keratinocytes in primary culture, relative to WT controls.
source: Moreover, PLA assays yielded evidence for decreased interactions between 14-3-3σ and YAP in Krt14 C373A keratinocytes in primary culture, relative to WT controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F), thereby extending the immunoprecipitation findings shown in Figure 4B.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The five cysteine residues present in human K14 are conserved in the mouse ortholog.
source: The five cysteine residues present in human K14 are conserved in the mouse ortholog (Lee et al., 2012), and cysteines at positions 4, 40, and 367 in human K14 participate in disulfide bonding (Feng and Coulombe, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012 and Feng and Coulombe, 2015a.

claim: Cysteines at positions 4, 40, and 367 in human K14 participate in disulfide bonding.
source: The five cysteine residues present in human K14 are conserved in the mouse ortholog (Lee et al., 2012), and cysteines at positions 4, 40, and 367 in human K14 participate in disulfide bonding (Feng and Coulombe, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feng and Coulombe, 2015a.

claim: Only 19.5% of GFP-K14WT-expressing keratinocytes exhibit nuclear YAP in the presence of calcium.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Sambandam et al., 2015), only 19.5% of GFP-K14WT-expressing keratinocytes exhibit nuclear YAP in the presence of calcium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B and citation to Sambandam et al., 2015.

claim: Cells expressing either a GFP-K14 cysteine free (CF) mutant, or a GFP-C367A single mutant, feature an abnormally high nuclear retention of YAP (83.8% and 81.9%, respectively).
source: By contrast, cells expressing either a GFP-K14 cysteine free (CF) mutant, or a GFP-C367A single mutant, feature an abnormally high nuclear retention of YAP (83.8% and 81.9%, respectively) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Restoring Cys367 in the K14-CF backbone (GFP-K14CF-C367 construct) rescued the abnormal nuclear retention of YAP, given that only 27.3% of transfected cells show YAP in the nucleus.
source: Restoring Cys367 in the K14-CF backbone (GFP-K14CF-C367 construct) rescued the abnormal nuclear retention of YAP, given that only 27.3% of transfected cells show YAP in the nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The stutter cysteine (C367 in human K14) is a calcium-dependent regulator of the subcellular partitioning of YAP in skin keratinocytes.
source: These findings directly implicate the stutter cysteine (C367 in human K14) as a calcium-dependent regulator of the subcellular partitioning of YAP in skin keratinocytes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: HeLa cells normally show low levels of K14 expression but respond well to K5-K14 co-transfection.
source: HeLa cells were selected because they are epithelia-derived, and grow and transfect well. HeLa cells normally show low levels of K14 expression (Moll et al., 1982) but respond well to K5-K14 co-transfection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moll et al., 1982 and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Transfection of a Ccn1 (Cyr61) gene promoter-driven Firefly luciferase plasmid led to a strong (~8 fold) induction of luciferase activity normalized to cells transfected with a reference Renilla luciferase plasmid.
source: Transfection of a Ccn1 (Cyr61) gene promoter-driven Firefly luciferase plasmid, previously shown to effectively report on YAP transcriptional activity (Ma et al., 2017), led to a strong (~8 fold) induction of luciferase activity normalized to cells transfected with a reference Renilla luciferase plasmid (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C and citation to Ma et al., 2017.

claim: Ccn1 promoter activity was significantly attenuated by co-expression of WT K14 along with assembly partner WT K5.
source: Consistent with K14's ability to retain YAP in the cytoplasm, Ccn1 promoter activity was significantly attenuated by co-expression of WT K14 along with assembly partner WT K5 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Activity of the Ccn1 promoter construct was much less affected when cysteine-free K14 (K14 CF) was co-expressed with WT K5.
source: In striking contrast, activity of the Ccn1 promoter construct was much less affected when cysteine-free K14 (K14 CF) was co-expressed with WT K5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The organization of filaments in HeLa cells co-expressing either K5 and K14WT or K5 and K14CF is comparable.
source: Of note, the organization of filaments in HeLa cells co-expressing either K5 and K14WT or K5 and K14CF is comparable (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YAP is a key effector of mechanosensing and mechanotransduction.
source: YAP is a key effector of mechanosensing and mechanotransduction (Dupont et al., 2011; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015; Panciera et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dupont et al., 2011; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015; Panciera et al., 2017.

claim: Cells experiencing tension often respond by enhancing determinants such as F-actin stress fibers, acto-myosin contraction, the recruitment of α-catenin and vinculin to adherens junctions.
source: Cells experiencing tension often respond by enhancing determinants such as F-actin stress fibers, acto-myosin contraction, the recruitment of α-catenin and vinculin to adherens junctions (Leckband and de Rooij, 2014; Yap et al., 2018), expression of lamin A/C in the nucleus (Swift et al., 2013), and frequency of binucleation (Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leckband and de Rooij, 2014; Yap et al., 2018.

claim: Cells experiencing tension often respond by enhancing expression of lamin A/C in the nucleus.
source: Cells experiencing tension often respond by enhancing determinants such as F-actin stress fibers, acto-myosin contraction, the recruitment of α-catenin and vinculin to adherens junctions (Leckband and de Rooij, 2014; Yap et al., 2018), expression of lamin A/C in the nucleus (Swift et al., 2013), and frequency of binucleation (Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Swift et al., 2013.

claim: Cells experiencing tension often respond by enhancing frequency of binucleation.
source: Cells experiencing tension often respond by enhancing determinants such as F-actin stress fibers, acto-myosin contraction, the recruitment of α-catenin and vinculin to adherens junctions (Leckband and de Rooij, 2014; Yap et al., 2018), expression of lamin A/C in the nucleus (Swift et al., 2013), and frequency of binucleation (Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cao et al., 2017.

claim: The immunostaining for α-catenin and for lamin A/C but not that for desmoglein 1 are markedly increased in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT controls.
source: In tail skin tissue sections, the immunostaining for α-catenin and for lamin A/C but not that for desmoglein 1 are markedly increased in Krt14 C373A mice relative to WT controls (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Epidermal keratinocytes are under altered tensile stress in Krt14 C373A epidermis.
source: Use of the a-18 antibody that recognizes a mechanosensitive epitope on α-catenin (Shimoyama et al., 1992) confirms that epidermal keratinocytes are under altered tensile stress in Krt14 C373A epidermis (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and citation to Shimoyama et al., 1992.

claim: The immunofluorescence signal for α-catenin, lamin A/C, F-actin stress fibers and phosphorylated myosin light chain II (pMLC Ser19) are each increased in Krt14 C373A relative to WT keratinocytes in primary culture.
source: We also find that the immunofluorescence signal for α-catenin, lamin A/C, F-actin stress fibers and phosphorylated myosin light chain II (pMLC Ser19) are each increased in Krt14 C373A relative to WT (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Krt14 C373A mutant keratinocytes show alterations in mechanosensing and/or mechanotransduction relative to WT.
source: Collectively these findings strongly suggest that, consistent with YAP misregulation (see Figure 5), Krt14 C373A mutant keratinocytes show alterations in mechanosensing and/or mechanotransduction relative to WT.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Residue cysteine 373 in mouse K14 partakes in regulating the balance between keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation in epidermis in vivo.
source: Our study establishes that residue cysteine 373 in mouse K14 partakes in regulating the balance between keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation in epidermis in vivo, and ultimately barrier function, in skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The loss of cysteine 373 results in profound alterations in the pattern of K14-dependent disulfide bonding in epidermis.
source: The loss of cysteine 373 results in profound alterations in the i) pattern of K14-dependent disulfide bonding in epidermis; ii) regulation of 14-3-3sigma and YAP in early-stage differentiating keratinocytes; and iii) several mechanosensitive readouts in the young adult epidermis in situ and newborn skin keratinocytes in primary culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The loss of cysteine 373 results in profound alterations in the regulation of 14-3-3sigma and YAP in early-stage differentiating keratinocytes.
source: The loss of cysteine 373 results in profound alterations in the i) pattern of K14-dependent disulfide bonding in epidermis; ii) regulation of 14-3-3sigma and YAP in early-stage differentiating keratinocytes; and iii) several mechanosensitive readouts in the young adult epidermis in situ and newborn skin keratinocytes in primary culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The loss of cysteine 373 results in profound alterations in several mechanosensitive readouts in the young adult epidermis in situ and newborn skin keratinocytes in primary culture.
source: The loss of cysteine 373 results in profound alterations in the i) pattern of K14-dependent disulfide bonding in epidermis; ii) regulation of 14-3-3sigma and YAP in early-stage differentiating keratinocytes; and iii) several mechanosensitive readouts in the young adult epidermis in situ and newborn skin keratinocytes in primary culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: K14-dependent disulfide bonding involving the conserved 'stutter cysteine' residue impacts cell architecture, mechanosensing and Hippo signaling at an early stage of epithelial differentiation in the epidermis.
source: Our findings support the conclusion that K14-dependent disulfide bonding involving the conserved 'stutter cysteine' residue impacts cell architecture, mechanosensing and Hippo signaling at an early stage of epithelial differentiation in the epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hippo signaling is inactive in most keratinocytes in the basal layer of epidermis.
source: Consistent with the literature, the model posits that Hippo signaling is inactive in most keratinocytes in the basal layer of epidermis (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Beverdam et al., 2013; Sambandam et al., 2015; Totaro et al., 2017), with YAP localizing to the nucleus given a specific level of cellular crowding and/or integrin-mediated adhesion to the extracellular matrix (Panciera et al., 2017; Elbediwy and Thompson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Beverdam et al., 2013; Sambandam et al., 2015; Totaro et al., 2017.

claim: YAP localizes to the nucleus in basal keratinocytes given a specific level of cellular crowding and/or integrin-mediated adhesion to the extracellular matrix.
source: Consistent with the literature, the model posits that Hippo signaling is inactive in most keratinocytes in the basal layer of epidermis (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Beverdam et al., 2013; Sambandam et al., 2015; Totaro et al., 2017), with YAP localizing to the nucleus given a specific level of cellular crowding and/or integrin-mediated adhesion to the extracellular matrix (Panciera et al., 2017; Elbediwy and Thompson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Panciera et al., 2017; Elbediwy and Thompson, 2018.

claim: In basal keratinocytes, K5-K14 filaments are organized in loose bundles that run alongside the nucleus.
source: In basal keratinocytes, K5-K14 filaments are organized in loose bundles that run alongside the nucleus (Coulombe et al., 1989; Lee et al., 2012) while 14-3-3σ occurs at low levels (Dellambra et al., 2000; Reichelt and Magin, 2002; Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coulombe et al., 1989; Lee et al., 2012.

claim: 14-3-3σ occurs at low levels in basal keratinocytes.
source: In basal keratinocytes, K5-K14 filaments are organized in loose bundles that run alongside the nucleus (Coulombe et al., 1989; Lee et al., 2012) while 14-3-3σ occurs at low levels (Dellambra et al., 2000; Reichelt and Magin, 2002; Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dellambra et al., 2000; Reichelt and Magin, 2002; Kim et al., 2006.

claim: Reception of differentiation-promoting cues triggers K14-dependent disulfide bonding and creates binding sites for 14-3-3 on K5-K14 filaments.
source: The first prediction of our model is that reception of differentiation-promoting cues triggers K14-dependent disulfide bonding and creates binding sites for 14-3-3 on K5-K14 filaments.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Binding sites for 14-3-3 on K5-K14 filaments likely occur via site-specific phosphorylation on K14.
source: The latter likely occurs via site-specific phosphorylation, on K14 (e.g., Inaba et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Inaba et al., 2018.

claim: Several reports converged in establishing a role for mitochondria-derived reactive oxygen species as a key trigger towards the initiation of terminal differentiation in keratinocytes of epidermis.
source: Several reports converged in establishing a role for mitochondria-derived reactive oxygen species as a key trigger towards the initiation of terminal differentiation in keratinocytes of epidermis (Tamiji et al., 2005; Bause et al., 2013; Hamanaka et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tamiji et al., 2005; Bause et al., 2013; Hamanaka et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondria-derived reactive oxygen species could non-enzymatically mediate K14-dependent disulfide bonding in the perinuclear cytoplasm of keratinocytes.
source: Such species could non-enzymatically mediate K14-dependent disulfide bonding in the perinuclear cytoplasm of keratinocytes (Suzuki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2019.

claim: Many type I keratins expressed in epidermis (e.g., K10, K16, K17) feature a cysteine residue at the location corresponding to codon 373 in mouse K14 and codon 367 in human K14.
source: Many type I keratins expressed in epidermis (e.g., K10, K16, K17) feature a cysteine residue at the location corresponding to codon 373 in mouse K14 and codon 367 in human K14 (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: KRT10 (human) and Krt10 (mouse) expression is turned on at the earliest stage of terminal differentiation.
source: First, KRT10 (human) and Krt10 (mouse) expression is turned on at the earliest stage of terminal differentiation (Woodcock-Mitchell et al., 1982; Schweizer et al., 1984), and the K10 protein features a structurally and biochemically equivalent Cys residue at position 401 and is capable of interacting with 14-3-3 (Wilker et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Woodcock-Mitchell et al., 1982; Schweizer et al., 1984.

claim: The K10 protein features a structurally and biochemically equivalent Cys residue at position 401 and is capable of interacting with 14-3-3.
source: First, KRT10 (human) and Krt10 (mouse) expression is turned on at the earliest stage of terminal differentiation (Woodcock-Mitchell et al., 1982; Schweizer et al., 1984), and the K10 protein features a structurally and biochemically equivalent Cys residue at position 401 and is capable of interacting with 14-3-3 (Wilker et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilker et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2010.

claim: The crystal structure of the interacting 2B segments of K1-K10 shows an overall fold identical to the K5(2B)-K14(2B) structure, including the presence of a trans-dimer, homotypic disulfide bond mediated by the stutter cysteine (C401) in K10.
source: Second, the crystal structure of the interacting 2B segments of K1-K10 (Bunick and Milstone, 2017) shows an overall fold identical to our original K5(2B)-K14(2B) structure (Lee et al., 2012), including the presence of a trans-dimer, homotypic disulfide bond mediated by the stutter cysteine (C401) in K10.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bunick and Milstone, 2017 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: K10 partakes in the formation of disulfide-dependent, dimer-sized species in skin keratinocytes.
source: Third, we previously showed that K10 partakes in the formation of disulfide-dependent, dimer-sized species in skin keratinocytes (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: The Krt10 null mouse exhibits a strong phenotype consisting of hyperproliferation, faster keratinocyte transit time, and impaired differentiation in the epidermis which correlates with a marked upregulation of 14-3-3sigma and c-Myc.
source: Fourth the Krt10 null mouse, described >15 years ago (Reichelt and Magin, 2002; Reichelt et al., 2004), exhibits a strong phenotype consisting of hyperproliferation, faster keratinocyte transit time, and impaired differentiation in the epidermis which, molecularly, correlates with a marked upregulation of 14-3-3sigma and c-Myc.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reichelt and Magin, 2002; Reichelt et al., 2004.

claim: MYC has been shown to be a bona fide YAP1 target gene.
source: MYC has since then been shown to be a bona fide YAP1 target gene (Schütte et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schütte et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2018.

claim: The newly-defined role for K14 in regulating the subcellular partitioning of YAP and onset of keratinocyte differentiation in epidermis is predicted to be picked up and maintained by K10 as differentiation proceeds.
source: Accordingly, our model (Figure 7A) predicts that the newly-defined role for K14 in regulating the subcellular partitioning of YAP and onset of keratinocyte differentiation in epidermis is picked up and maintained by K10 as differentiation proceeds.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the experimental data and literature.

claim: The network of keratin filaments proximal to the nucleus acts as a key docking site for 14-3-3/YAP complexes during keratinocyte delamination and differentiation.
source: They suggest that the network of keratin filaments proximal to the nucleus acts as a key docking site for 14-3-3/YAP complexes during keratinocyte delamination and differentiation, taking on a role that has been held to this point by integrin-based adhesion sites (Elbediwy et al., 2016) and adherens junctions (via alpha-catenin; (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Silvis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental data and citations to Elbediwy et al., 2016; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Silvis et al., 2011.

claim: A disulfide bonding-rich perinuclear network of keratin filaments could afford protection to the nucleus and the genome during delamination.
source: In addition, a disulfide bonding-rich perinuclear network of keratin filaments could also afford protection to the nucleus and the genome during delamination (Lee et al., 2012), thus extending the known role of K5-K14 IFs in providing mechanical support in basal keratinocytes (Coulombe et al., 1991a; Ramms et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012; Coulombe et al., 1991a; Ramms et al., 2013.

claim: Keratinocyte delamination and differentiation in epidermis together entail a profound reorganization of cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion, and of F-actin and microtubule organization.
source: Besides, keratinocyte delamination and differentiation in epidermis together entail a profound reorganization of cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion, and of F-actin and microtubule organization (Sumigray and Lechler, 2015; Muroyama and Lechler, 2017; Miroshnikova et al., 2018; Rübsam et al., 2018; Wickström and Niessen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sumigray and Lechler, 2015; Muroyama and Lechler, 2017; Miroshnikova et al., 2018; Rübsam et al., 2018; Wickström and Niessen, 2018.

claim: YAP's role as a transcription factor requires its binding to TEAD protein, which is itself stably bound to the promoter of its target genes in a sequence-specific fashion in the nucleus.
source: YAP's role as a transcription factor requires its binding to TEAD protein, which is itself stably bound to the promoter of its target genes in a sequence-specific fashion in the nucleus (Vassilev et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vassilev et al., 2001.

claim: Keratin genes expressed in dividing basal cells of epidermis, for example the type I Krt14 and Krt15 and type II Krt5, are likely YAP target genes given the presence of consensus-matching TEAD binding sites occurring in open chromatin regions in the absence of calcium.
source: The combination of DNAse one hypersensitivity mapping, ATAC-seq mapping, and presence of TEAD binding sites (in either orientation) on DNA (5'- CATTCC-3'; Heinz et al., 2010) suggests that keratin genes expressed in dividing basal cells of epidermis, for example the type I Krt14 and Krt15 and type II Krt5, are likely YAP target genes given the presence of consensus-matching TEAD binding sites occurring in open chromatin regions in the absence of calcium (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from ENCODE data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2, and citation to Heinz et al., 2010.

claim: The chromatin surrounding keratin genes expressed in dividing basal cells becomes non-accessible in the presence of calcium.
source: ENCODE data convey that the chromatin surrounding these genes becomes non-accessible in the presence of calcium (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and 2), which promotes differentiation (Hennings et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is based on ENCODE data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and 2, and citation to Hennings et al., 1980.

claim: Keratin genes expressed in differentiating keratinocytes of epidermis, including the type I Krt10 and type Krt1 and Krt2, do not feature proximal TEAD binding sites and thus are not likely to be transcribed in a TEAD/YAP-dependent fashion in epidermis.
source: Keratin genes expressed in differentiating keratinocytes of epidermis, including the type I Krt10 and type Krt1 and Krt2, do not feature proximal TEAD binding sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2) and thus are not likely to be transcribed in a TEAD/YAP-dependent fashion in epidermis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from ENCODE data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The YAP1 and TEAD genes (human) are themselves poised to be positively regulated by YAP in progenitor keratinocytes.
source: The YAP1 and TEAD genes (human) are themselves poised to be positively regulated by YAP in progenitor keratinocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from ENCODE data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The YAP/TEAD axis may be set up to promote unabated cell proliferation in a fast-renewing epithelium such as epidermis until two post-translational events converging on K14 protein, phosphorylation and disulfide bonding, would lead to YAP protein sequestration in the cytoplasm and inactivation of the YAP/TEAD axis as part of a regulated negative feedback loop.
source: Accordingly, the YAP/TEAD axis may be set up to promote unabated cell proliferation in a fast-renewing epithelium such as epidermis until two post-translational events converging on K14 protein, phosphorylation and disulfide bonding, would lead to YAP protein sequestration in the cytoplasm and inactivation of the YAP/TEAD axis as part of a regulated negative feedback loop, enacted at the time of entry into differentiation in epidermis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental data and ENCODE analysis.

claim: The perinuclear enrichment of keratin IFs, which is promoted by K14-dependent disulfide bonding, is poised to increase the local concentration of binding sites for 14-3-3σ and YAP near the nucleus.
source: First, the perinuclear enrichment of keratin IFs, which is promoted by K14-dependent disulfide bonding, is poised to increase the local concentration of binding sites for 14-3-3σ and YAP near the nucleus (simple mass action law).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The occurrence of K14-dependent disulfides may create an optimal binding interface for 14-3-3σ and YAP in the cytoplasm residing proximal to the nucleus.
source: Second, the occurrence of K14-dependent disulfides may create an optimal binding interface for 14-3-3σ and YAP in the cytoplasm residing proximal to the nucleus.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The nucleus is known to function as a mechanosensor.
source: Third, the nucleus is known to function as a mechanosensor (Cao et al., 2017), and local forces impacted by the perinuclear network of keratin filaments could alter the mechanical gating of YAP across nuclear pores (Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cao et al., 2017.

claim: Local forces impacted by the perinuclear network of keratin filaments could alter the mechanical gating of YAP across nuclear pores.
source: Third, the nucleus is known to function as a mechanosensor (Cao et al., 2017), and local forces impacted by the perinuclear network of keratin filaments could alter the mechanical gating of YAP across nuclear pores (Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by a citation to Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017.
